sentences.text: The night of the Mid-Autumn Festival, the town was almost impossibly beautiful.
Every building was hung with lanterns.
Every window was hung with lanterns.
The trees in the square were hung with lanterns.
The river was full of small candle-lanterns that people were setting afloat.
There must have been ten thousand people in the old town.
Mai stood in the middle of the town square, in her best áo dài, holding the practice string in her hands to stop them from shaking.
Her parents were at the front of the crowd.
Her father waved at her.
She waved back.
She was terrified.
The fish lantern was on a small wooden platform in the center of the square.
It was even bigger than Mai had realized.
Ông Lâm was checking every fin, every string, every candle inside.
He worked slowly and calmly.
When he was ready, he came over to Mai.
He was small.
Mai had realized, in the last three weeks, that she was almost as tall as he was.
"Mai," he said.
He held out the string — the real string, the one attached to the finished fish lantern.
"Take it.
Feel it in your hands.
Breathe.
Do you remember what I told you." She said, "Yes." "What did I tell you." "Do not fight it.
Move with it.
Relax my shoulders.
Breathe from my belly, not my chest.
Do not lock my knees.
Watch the tail of the lantern, not the string." Ông Lâm smiled.
"Yes.
Very good.
Come.
It is time."
He led her onto the wooden platform.
He lit the small candles inside the fish, one by one.
The lantern began to glow — a warm orange from the inside, so beautiful Mai wanted to cry.
He checked the string.
He nodded to her.
He stepped back.
The whole square went quiet.
Ten thousand people stopped talking.
Mai stood on the platform, alone, holding the string that held the fish lantern.
The mayor of Hoi An made a small speech that Mai did not really hear.
Then he said her name.
Then he said, in a loud voice, "Release the lantern!"
The lantern rose.
Mai had known it would rise — that was the point of it, the heat of the candles made it fly — but she had not fully believed it until it did.
It lifted off its stand slowly, and then more quickly, and then it was floating above her head.
She adjusted her grip.
She let out the string, hand over hand, the way Ông Lâm had shown her.
She let it rise.
She did not fight it.
She breathed.
She watched the tail.
The lantern floated up above the crowd.
It went up maybe fifteen meters.
Then it stopped rising and it started to drift — the wind was pulling it toward the river.
Mai turned as it drifted.
She kept the string tight but not too tight.
She could feel the lantern moving — as if she was holding a small living thing on a leash, exactly as Ông Lâm had said.
It was heavy and light at the same time.
It wanted to go.
She let it go, but she also held it.
Both were true.
The wind pulled the lantern out over the river.
Mai walked with it.
Ông Lâm was behind her, watching.
He did not touch her.
He let her do it.
The crowd followed her — a long line of people walking with her along the bank of the river.
The lantern floated above the water.
She could see, from below, its silhouette against the huge round moon that had risen over the town.
It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen in her life.
And she was holding the string that held it.
And it was not fighting her.
She was not fighting it.
They were moving together.
It flew for maybe eighteen minutes.
Then it began to descend — the candles were burning low.
Mai could feel the string get slack, then tight, then slack.
She let it drift down.
The lantern began to lose its shape as the silk started to burn.
Small flames appeared on its sides.
Mai kept walking.
The fish lantern floated down over the river.
It touched the water.
It sat on the surface, still glowing.
Then, slowly, the paper burned away, and the bamboo frame — freed of its silk — began to sink.
The last candles guttered.
The fish lantern went dark.
It floated on the water for another minute, half-submerged.
Then it slipped under.
Mai stood at the water's edge with the empty string in her hands.
She did not move.
Ông Lâm came up beside her.
He put his hand on her shoulder.
He said, in his soft voice, "You did it.
You did it perfectly.
The whole town will remember.
My teacher would have been proud.
I am proud." Mai said, quietly, "It is gone." "Yes," said Ông Lâm.
"It is gone.
That is the whole point.
You know that.
You knew that when you agreed.
You did it anyway.
That is what a person like you does."
Mai stood at the river for a while longer.
The crowd began to disperse.
Her parents came up to her and hugged her.
Her mother was crying.
Her father was smiling in a way she had not seen before.
She hugged them back.
She was very tired.
She was also — she realized — very happy.
Ông Lâm was standing a little way off, letting her family have her.
When she looked over at him, he was watching her.
He smiled.
She smiled back.
She understood that in twenty years, or forty years, or whenever it was, it would be her turn to choose the next person.
She understood that she would have to look, for a long time, before she found them.
She understood that this was the whole tradition — one person, choosing another person, in the crowd, over years.
She thought — I can do that.
I can watch, when the time comes.
I will know who they are, the way he knew who I was.
